title: PSTAT 126: Regression Analysis
text:
This course covers the theory and application of linear and multiple regression, with an emphasis on using statistical computing to solve real-world problems. Topics include simple and multiple linear regression, analysis of residuals, transformations, variable and model selection (including stepwise regression), and analysis of covariance. All computing is done in R.
By the end of the quarter, you will be able to formulate, fit, and interpret regression models, diagnose violations of model assumptions, handle outliers, leverage points and multicollinearity, apply appropriate transformations, implement variable selection methods, and perform statistical inference and prediction.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Review: The Simple Linear Model
From Monday, the simple linear regression model is:
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \quad \varepsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\]

\(\beta_1\) is a comparison between units
The fitted line \(\widehat{y} = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x\) summarizes the relationship

Today: How do we estimate \(\widehat{\beta}_0\), \(\widehat{\beta}_1\), and \(\sigma\) from data?

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of today you will be able to:

Explain the least squares criterion and apply it conceptually
State the OLS formulas for the slope and intercept
Compute and interpret fitted values and residuals
Interpret the residual standard deviation \(\widehat{\sigma}\) and \(R^2\)
Explain what a standard error measures
Use lm() in R to fit a simple linear regression and read its output

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
section: How Do We Fit a Line?
text: How Do We Fit a Line?

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
The Problem of Fitting
Given data \((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)\), infinitely many lines pass through or near the points.
We need a criterion to select the “best” line.
Intuition: The best line should make prediction errors as small as possible across all observations simultaneously.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Residuals: Measuring Prediction Error
For a candidate line with intercept \(a\) and slope \(b\), the residual for observation \(i\) is:
\[e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i = y_i - (a + b x_i)\]

\(\hat{y}_i = a + bx_i\): the fitted value (what the line predicts)
\(e_i > 0\): observed point is above the line
\(e_i < 0\): observed point is below the line

A good line has small residuals throughout.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
The Least Squares Criterion
From the previous slide, \(e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i\). Since the candidate line predicts \(\widehat{y}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\), substituting gives:
\[e_i = y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\]
So the Residual Sum of Squares is:
\[\text{RSS}(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2\]
Goal: choose \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) to minimize RSS.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Deriving the OLS Estimators
Minimize RSS by taking partial derivatives with respect to \(a\) and \(b\), setting them to zero, and solving:
\[\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\]
\[\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\]






Note


The OLS line always passes through the point \((\bar{x},\, \bar{y})\).

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
A Useful Rewrite
The OLS slope can also be written as:
\[\hat{\beta}_1 = r \cdot \frac{s_y}{s_x}\]
where \(r\) is the sample correlation between \(x\) and \(y\), and \(s_x\), \(s_y\) are sample standard deviations.

When \(r = 0\): slope is 0 — no linear relationship
When \(|r| = 1\): all points lie exactly on a line
The sign of \(\hat{\beta}_1\) always equals the sign of \(r\)

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
section: Fitting the Election Model in R
text:
Fitting the Election Model in R

hibbs <- read.table("hibbs.dat", header = TRUE)
fit   <- lm(vote ~ growth, data = hibbs)
summary(fit)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)  46.248      1.623   28.50  < 2e-16 ***
growth        3.061      0.710    4.31  0.00076 ***

Residual standard error: 3.763 on 14 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared: 0.5700

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Reading the lm() Output







Term
What it means




(Intercept)
\(\widehat{\beta}_0 = 46.2\): predicted vote share when growth = 0%


growth
\(\widehat{\beta}_1 = 3.1\): predicted change in vote share per 1% more income growth


Std. Error
Estimated standard error of each coefficient


t value
Coefficient estimate divided by its standard error


Pr(>|t|)
p-value for the hypothesis \(H_0: \beta = 0\)


Residual standard error

Multiple R-squared
\(R^2 = 0.57\): fraction of variance in \(y\) explained by the model

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text: Residuals and Model Fit

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Accessing Residuals in R

residuals(fit)   # e_i = y_i - y_hat_i
fitted(fit)      # y_hat_i = beta0_hat + beta1_hat * x_i

# Residual plot
plot(fitted(fit), residuals(fit),
     xlab = "Fitted values",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs. Fitted")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "gray50")

A well-fitted model has residuals that are centered at zero with no systematic pattern.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Estimating \(\sigma\)
The true error variance \(\sigma^2\) is unknown — we estimate it from the residuals:
\[\widehat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\text{RSS}}{n - 2} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{y}_i)^2}{n - 2}\]
We divide by \(n - 2\) — not \(n\) — because we estimated two parameters (\(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\)) from the data, using up 2 degrees of freedom.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
What Does \(\hat{\sigma}\) Tell Us?
\(\hat{\sigma}\) is the residual standard deviation — the typical size of prediction errors, on the scale of \(y\).
For the election model: \(\hat{\sigma} = 3.76\) percentage points.
Interpretation: Even with the best linear prediction using income growth, vote shares typically deviate from predictions by about 3.8 percentage points.






Tip


Compare \(\hat{\sigma}\) to the spread of \(y\) to assess predictive accuracy. A small \(\hat{\sigma}\) relative to the range of \(y\) indicates a useful model.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
\(R^2\): Proportion of Variance Explained
\[R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{RSS}}{\text{TSS}} = 1 - \frac{\displaystyle\sum(y_i - \widehat{y}_i)^2}{\displaystyle\sum(y_i - \bar{y})^2}\]

TSS = Total Sum of Squares — variance in \(y\) if we ignored \(x\) entirely
\(R^2 = 0\): the model explains nothing; predicting \(\bar{y}\) is just as good
\(R^2 = 1\): the model explains everything; residuals are all zero
Election model: \(R^2 = 0.57\) — income growth explains 57% of the variation in vote share







Caution


High \(R^2\) does not mean the model is correct or causal — it only measures linear fit.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text: Standard Errors

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
What is a Standard Error?
A standard error measures the precision of a sample estimate.
Imagine drawing many independent samples of size \(n\) from the same population and computing \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) each time. The standard deviation of those estimates across samples is the standard error of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\).
\[\text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\widehat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}} = \frac{\widehat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2}}\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
What Makes Standard Errors Smaller?
\[\text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\widehat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2}}\]
Standard errors are smaller (more precise estimates) when:

\(\widehat{\sigma}\) is small — less noise in the data
Predictors \(x\) are more spread out — more information about the slope
Sample size \(n\) is larger — more data overall

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Confidence Intervals for Coefficients
A 95% confidence interval for \(\beta_1\) is:
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 \pm t_{n-2,\,0.025} \cdot \text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_1)\]
For the election model (\(n = 16\), \(t_{14, 0.025} \approx 2.14\)):
\[3.06 \pm 2.14 \times 0.71 \approx (1.54,\; 4.58)\]
Interpretation: We are 95% confident the true slope lies between 1.54 and 4.58 — a 1% increase in income growth is associated with between 1.5 and 4.6 more percentage points of vote share.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text: Regression as Comparison

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Comparing Two Groups as Regression
Regression is a generalization of simpler statistical comparisons.
Comparing a single mean: regress \(y\) on just a constant: \[y_i = \mu + \varepsilon_i \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \widehat{\mu} = \bar{y}\]
Comparing two groups: let \(x_i \in \{0, 1\}\) be a binary group indicator: \[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i\]

\(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y}_{\text{group 0}}\)
\(\widehat{\beta}_1 = \bar{y}_{\text{group 1}} - \bar{y}_{\text{group 0}}\)

This is algebraically equivalent to a two-sample \(t\)-test (assuming equal variances).

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Regression Generalizes the \(t\)-test

# Suppose x is a binary 0/1 indicator (e.g., treatment vs. control)
t.test(y ~ x, var.equal = TRUE)

# Produces the same estimate as:
lm(y ~ x)

Regression is strictly more general — it can:

Handle continuous predictors
Adjust for additional variables simultaneously (multiple regression)
Accommodate more than two groups via indicator coding

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Making Predictions
Given a new observation with predictor value \(x^*\), the predicted outcome is:
\[\widehat{y}^* = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x^*\]
Example: What vote share does the model predict when income growth = 2%?
\[\widehat{y} = 46.2 + 3.1 \times 2 = 52.4\%\]






Extrapolation


Predicting far outside the range of the observed \(x\) values is unreliable. The linear relationship may not hold beyond the data.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Brief Intro: Fake-Data Simulation
A powerful way to validate our fitting procedure: simulate data from a known model, then check whether we can recover the true parameters.

set.seed(42)
n     <- 50
x     <- runif(n, min = 0, max = 10)

# True (known) parameters
beta0 <- 2
beta1 <- 3
sigma <- 5

y   <- beta0 + beta1 * x + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sigma)
fit <- lm(y ~ x)
coef(fit)  # should be close to (2, 3)

If estimates are far from the truth on simulated data, something is wrong with our procedure.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Summary

Least squares: OLS picks \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) to minimize \(\text{RSS} = \sum(y_i - \widehat{y}_i)^2\)
Normal equations give closed-form solutions: \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}\), \(\;\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\)
Residuals \(e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i\) measure how far each observation falls from the fitted line
Property 1 (Linearity): both estimators are linear combinations of \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\)
Property 2 (Unbiasedness): \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \beta_0\) and \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\)
Property 3 (Known variances): \(\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \sigma^2/S_{xx}\), \(\;\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \sigma^2(1/n + \bar{x}^2/S_{xx})\)
Property 4 (Gauss-Markov): OLS is BLUE — smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Francis Galton and Heredity
In the 1880s, Francis Galton studied the relationship between parents’ heights and their children’s heights.
His finding: Tall parents tend to have taller children who are shorter than the parents. Short parents tend to have shorter children who are taller than the parents.
Children’s heights “regressed” back toward the population mean.
This is the origin of the word “regression.”

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Pearson & Lee (1903)
Karl Pearson and Alice Lee measured heights of 1,078 father-son pairs.Using the data they collected, they found that:
\[\widehat{\text{son's height}} = 33.9 + 0.51 \times \text{father's height}\]

A father 1 inch above average \(\Rightarrow\) son predicted ~0.51 inches above average
The slope is less than 1: sons are pulled toward the mean relative to fathers
This is regression to the mean in its original form

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
section: What is Regression to the Mean?
text:
What is Regression to the Mean?
Key insight: Extreme values on one measurement tend to be less extreme on a subsequent measurement — not because of any real change, but because of random variation.






The Regression Fallacy


Mistaking regression to the mean for a real causal effect.



Examples:

Students who score very high on a pretest score lower on a retest, on average
Athletes who have exceptional seasons tend to regress the following year
Patients who seek treatment when symptoms are worst often improve — even without effective treatment

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
section: Why Does Regression to the Mean Happen?
text:
Why Does Regression to the Mean Happen?
Think of an observed score as composed of signal and noise:
\[x_{\text{observed}} = \mu_{\text{true}} + \varepsilon_{\text{random}}\]
When you select a very high observation, you’re also selecting a large positive error \(\varepsilon\). On a second measurement, that error is likely to be smaller — pulling the score back toward the mean.
This is a statistical artifact, not a causal mechanism.

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Regression Coefficients Describe Comparisons
A regression slope \(\hat{\beta}_1\) compares groups of units that differ by 1 unit in \(x\).
\(\hat{\beta}_1\) is the estimated average difference in \(y\) between two otherwise-similar observations where \(x\) differs by 1 unit.






Correlation \(\neq\) Causation


Regression coefficients describe associations in data. They do not, by themselves, establish causal relationships.

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Why “Effect” Language Can Mislead
Consider: “Each year of education increases income by $5,000.”
This phrasing implies a causal mechanism — that giving someone more education would change their income by $5,000.
What the regression actually estimates:

“People with one more year of education earn, on average, $5,000 more than people with one fewer year of education.”

The difference matters when drawing policy conclusions.

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
A Better Framing


Avoid:
“Education increases income by $5,000.”

Prefer:
“Comparing people who differ by one year of education, those with more education earn $5,000 more on average.”

Regression describes comparisons across units in the data. Causal claims require additional study design considerations beyond this course.

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Why Minimize Squared Errors?

Wang, PSTAT 126 Notes (hand1.pdf), p. 17 · ROS Ch. 8.1

We need a rule to pick the “best” \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\). The natural goal: make prediction errors small across all observations simultaneously.
The residual for observation \(i\) is \(e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\).
Why square the residuals rather than just summing them?

Positive and negative errors cancel — the sum \(\sum e_i = 0\) for any line through \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\), so it carries no useful information
Squaring penalizes large errors more than small ones
The squared criterion has a clean, closed-form solution

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
The Least Squares Criterion

Wang, PSTAT 126 Notes (hand1.pdf), p. 17 · ROS Ch. 8.1

From the previous slide, \(e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\). Since the candidate line predicts \(\hat{y}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\), substituting gives:
\[e_i = y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\]
So the Residual Sum of Squares is:
\[\text{RSS}(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2\]
Goal: choose \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\) to minimize RSS.

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
The OLS Estimators

Wang, PSTAT 126 Notes (hand1.pdf), p. 18 · ROS Ch. 8.1

Solving the normal equations yields:
\[\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\]
\[\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\]






Note


The OLS line always passes through \((\bar{x},\, \bar{y})\).

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Connection to Correlation

Wang, PSTAT 126 Notes (hand1.pdf), p. 21

The OLS slope has a useful rewrite in terms of correlation:
\[\hat{\beta}_1 = r \cdot \frac{s_y}{s_x}\]
where \(r\) is the sample correlation between \(x\) and \(y\), and \(s_x\), \(s_y\) are sample standard deviations.

The sign of \(\hat{\beta}_1\) always equals the sign of \(r\)
When \(r = 0\): slope is 0 — no linear relationship
When \(|r| = 1\): all points lie exactly on a line — perfect fit

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Properties of the OLS Estimators

Wang, PSTAT 126 Notes (hand1.pdf), pp. 23–31 · ROS Ch. 8.1


Linear — \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\) are linear functions of \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\)
Unbiased — \(\mathbb{E}(\hat{\beta}_0) = \beta_0\) and \(\mathbb{E}(\hat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\): on average, the estimates recover the true parameters
Known variances: \[\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_0) = \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\]
Gauss-Markov (BLUE) — OLS estimators have the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators. No other unbiased linear estimator can do better.

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Estimating \(\sigma^2\)

Wang, PSTAT 126 Notes (hand1.pdf), p. 37 · ROS Ch. 8.1

The error variance \(\sigma^2\) is unknown — we estimate it from the residuals.
Residual Sum of Squares (SSE): \[\text{SSE} = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\]
Mean Squared Error (MSE) = unbiased estimate of \(\sigma^2\): \[\hat{\sigma}^2 = \text{MSE} = \frac{\text{SSE}}{n - 2}\]
We divide by \(n - 2\) (not \(n\)) because estimating \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\) uses 2 degrees of freedom. It can be shown that \(\mathbb{E}(\text{MSE}) = \sigma^2\).

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
How do we pick \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\)?
We need a rule to pick the “best” \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\). To do so, we want to make prediction errors small across all observations simultaneously.
The residual for observation \(i\) is: \[e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\]
where \(\hat{y}_i\) (“y-hat sub \(i\)”) is the predicted value \(\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x_i\)
To find the best line, we minimize the Residual Sum of Squares: \[\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\]
We square the residuals so positive and negative errors don’t cancel, and so large errors are penalized more heavily.

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
The Normal Equations

Wang, PSTAT 126 Notes (hand1.pdf), p. 17 · ROS Ch. 8.1

RSS is a smooth function of \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\), so we minimize by calculus. Setting both partial derivatives to zero gives the normal equations:
\[\frac{\partial \text{RSS}}{\partial \beta_0} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0\]
\[\frac{\partial \text{RSS}}{\partial \beta_1} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0\]






Note


The first equation says the residuals sum to zero — the line is centered on the data. The second says the residuals are uncorrelated with \(x\) — no systematic trend is left over.

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Solving the Normal Equations

Wang, PSTAT 126 Notes (hand1.pdf), p. 18

Step 1 — solve equation 1 for \(\hat{\beta}_0\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; n\bar{y} - n\beta_0 - n\beta_1\bar{x} = 0\]
\[\boxed{\hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1\bar{x}}\]
Step 2 — substitute into equation 2 and solve for \(\hat{\beta}_1\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0\]
Replace \(\beta_0\) with \(\bar{y} - \beta_1\bar{x}\) and rearrange:
\[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y} = \beta_1\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2\right)\]
\[\boxed{\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y}}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}}\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
How do we pick \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\)?
We need a rule to pick the “best” \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\). To do so, we want to make prediction errors small across all observations simultaneously.
The residual for observation \(i\) is: \[e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i\]
where \(\widehat{y}_i\) is the predicted value \(\widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i\)
To find the best line, we minimize the Residual Sum of Squares: \[\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{y}_i)^2\]
We square the residuals so positive and negative errors don’t cancel, and so large errors are penalized more heavily.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
The Normal Equations
We have 2 unknowns (\(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\)) and need 2 equations to pin them down.
Setting \(\dfrac{\partial \text{RSS}}{\partial \beta_0} = 0\) and \(\dfrac{\partial \text{RSS}}{\partial \beta_1} = 0\) each gives one equation — together they form a system of two linear equations called the normal equations.
Recall: \(\text{RSS}(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2\)
Strategy: differentiate RSS with respect to each parameter, set each derivative to zero, then use the chain rule and summation rule to simplify.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Solving the Normal Equations

Wang, PSTAT 126 Notes (hand1.pdf), p. 18

Step 1 — solve equation 1 for \(\widehat{\beta}_0\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; n\bar{y} - n\beta_0 - n\beta_1\bar{x} = 0\]
\[\boxed{\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}}\]
Step 2 — substitute into equation 2 and solve for \(\widehat{\beta}_1\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0\]
Replace \(\beta_0\) with \(\bar{y} - \beta_1\bar{x}\) and rearrange:
\[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y} = \beta_1\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2\right)\]
\[\boxed{\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y}}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}}\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
The OLS Estimators
Solving the normal equations yields:
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\]
\[\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\]
where:
\[S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}) \quad \text{(co-variation of } x \text{ and } y \text{ around their means)}\]
\[S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \quad \text{(total spread of } x \text{ around its mean)}\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Connection to Correlation
The OLS slope has a useful rewrite in terms of correlation:
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = r \cdot \frac{s_y}{s_x}\]
where \(r\) is the sample correlation between \(x\) and \(y\), and \(s_x\), \(s_y\) are sample standard deviations.

The sign of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) always equals the sign of \(r\)
When \(r = 0\) \(\rightarrow\) slope is 0 \(\rightarrow\) no linear relationship
When \(|r| = 1\) \(\rightarrow\) all points lie exactly on a line \(\rightarrow\) perfect fit

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Properties of the OLS Estimators

Notation: \(S_{xx} = \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i - \bar{x})^2\) — total spread of the predictor; \(\sigma^2\) — true (unknown) error variance; \(\mathbb{E}(\cdot)\) — expected value; \(\text{Var}(\cdot)\) — variance.


Linear: \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) are linear functions of \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\)
Unbiased: \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \beta_0\) and \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\) — on average, the estimates recover the true parameters
Known variances: \[\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\]
Gauss-Markov (BLUE): OLS has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators — no other such estimator can do better.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Estimating \(\sigma^2\)
The error variance \(\sigma^2\) is unknown so we estimate it from the residuals.
Residual Sum of Squares (RSS): \[\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{y}_i)^2\]
Mean Squared Error (MSE) = unbiased estimate of \(\sigma^2\): \[\widehat{\sigma}^2 = \text{MSE} = \frac{\text{RSS}}{n - 2}\]
We divide by \(n - 2\) (not \(n\)) because estimating \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) uses 2 degrees of freedom. It can be shown that \(\mathbb{E}(\text{MSE}) = \sigma^2\).

title: Lecture 1: What is Regression?
text:
Inference vs. Prediction
Two distinct goals for regression:
Inference: understand how and why variables are related

Focus: the coefficients \(\beta_0, \beta_1\)
Questions: Is there a relationship? How strong? In what direction?
Example: Does income growth affect vote share, and by how much?

Prediction: produce accurate forecasts for new observations

Focus: the fitted value \(\widehat{y}\)
Questions: Given \(\widehat{x}\), what is our best guess for \(\widehat{y}\)?
Example: What vote share do we expect when income growth is 2%?

What Does \(\widehat{\sigma}\) Tell Us?
\(\widehat{\sigma}\) is the residual standard deviation — the typical size of prediction errors, on the scale of \(y\).
For the election model: \(\widehat{\sigma} = 3.76\) percentage points.
Interpretation: Even with the best linear prediction using income growth, vote shares typically deviate from predictions by about 3.8 percentage points.






Tip


Compare \(\widehat{\sigma}\) to the spread of \(y\) to assess predictive accuracy. A small \(\widehat{\sigma}\) relative to the range of \(y\) indicates a useful model.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Expanding the Normal Equations
Distribute the \(\sum\) across each term, using \(\sum \beta_0 = n\beta_0\) (a constant summed \(n\) times) and \(\sum \beta_1 x_i = \beta_1 \sum x_i\) (constant pulled out):
\[\sum y_i - n\beta_0 - \beta_1\sum x_i = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad n\beta_0 \;+\; \beta_1\sum x_i \;=\; \sum y_i\] \[\sum x_i y_i - \beta_0\sum x_i - \beta_1\sum x_i^2 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \beta_0\sum x_i \;+\; \beta_1\sum x_i^2 \;=\; \sum x_i y_i\]
These are just two linear equations in two unknowns (\(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\)) — solvable with algebra, which is exactly what the next slide does.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
section: A Note on Derivatives with Summations
text:
A Note on Derivatives with Summations
When taking derivatives inside a sum, constants come out and sums distribute:
\[\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2\]
Apply the chain rule to each term, then use:

\(\sum \beta_0 = n\beta_0\) — a constant summed \(n\) times
\(\sum \beta_1 x_i = \beta_1 \sum x_i\) — pull the constant out

This is why the partial derivatives simplify cleanly into the normal equations.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Mini Refresher: Derivatives
Power rule: \(\frac{d}{dx} x^n = nx^{n-1}\)
Chain rule: \(\frac{d}{dx} f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)\)
Partial derivatives: treat all other variables as constants and differentiate with respect to one variable at a time.
Example: \(\dfrac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0}(y - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x)^2 = 2(y - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x) \cdot (-1)\)

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Mini Refresher: Summation Rules
Derivatives through sums: \[\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(\beta_0) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0} f_i(\beta_0)\]
Constants in sums:

\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n c = nc\) — a constant summed \(n\) times is just \(n \times c\)
\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n c \cdot x_i = c\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\) — a constant factor pulls out of the sum







Note


These are all we need to minimize RSS — apply the chain rule, pass the derivative through the sum, set to zero, and simplify.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Solving the Normal Equations: Step 1
Solve equation 1 for \(\widehat{\beta}_0\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; n\bar{y} - n\beta_0 - n\beta_1\bar{x} = 0\]
\[\boxed{\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}}\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Solving the Normal Equations: Step 2
Substitute into equation 2 and solve for \(\widehat{\beta}_1\):
Start with equation 2 and distribute the sum: \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - \beta_0\sum_{i=1}^n x_i - \beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 = 0\]
Substitute \(\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \beta_1\bar{x}\) and use \(\sum x_i = n\bar{x}\): \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - (\bar{y} - \beta_1\bar{x})\,n\bar{x} - \beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 = 0\]
Expand the multiplication: \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y} + n\bar{x}^2\beta_1 - \beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 = 0\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Solving the Normal Equations: Step 2 (cont.)
Collect \(\beta_1\) terms on the right: \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y} = \beta_1\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2\right)\]
Divide both sides by \(\left(\sum x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2\right)\):
\[\boxed{\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y}}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}}\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Equivalent Form of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\)
The numerator and denominator have a cleaner equivalent form. Expanding \(\sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})\):
\[\sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}) = \sum x_iy_i - \bar{y}\sum x_i - \bar{x}\sum y_i + n\bar{x}\bar{y}\]
Since \(\sum x_i = n\bar{x}\) and \(\sum y_i = n\bar{y}\):
\[= \sum x_iy_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y} - n\bar{x}\bar{y} + n\bar{x}\bar{y} = \sum x_iy_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y}\]
The same identity holds for the denominator: \(\displaystyle\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2 = \sum x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2\)
So the two forms are equivalent. We will use the simpler form on the next slide.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
The Normal Equations
We start with computing the derivatives and dividing by \(-2\):


\[\frac{\partial RSS}{\partial \beta_0}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 =0\]

\[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial RSS}{\partial \beta_0}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 = 0\]


\[\sum_{i=1}^{n} 2(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) * (-1)= 0\]


\[ -2 * \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0\]


\[\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0\]


\[\frac{\partial RSS}{\partial \beta_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 =0\]

\[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial RSS}{\partial \beta_1}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 = 0\]


\[\sum_{i=1}^{n} 2(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) * (-x_i)= 0\]


\[ -2 * \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0\]


\[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0\]








Note


Eq. 1 says: the residuals sum to zero — no systematic over- or under-prediction across all observations.
Eq. 2 says: the residuals have no linear relationship with \(x\) — the model has captured everything that \(x\) can linearly explain.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
The Normal Equations: Derivation


Set \(\partial\text{RSS}/\partial\beta_0 = 0\): \[\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 = 0\]

Pass derivative through sum (summation rule): \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 = 0\]


Chain rule: \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} 2(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) \cdot (-1) = 0\]


Factor out \(-2\), then divide both sides by \(-2\): \[\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0\]


Set \(\partial\text{RSS}/\partial\beta_1 = 0\): \[\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 = 0\]

Pass derivative through sum (summation rule): \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_1}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 = 0\]


Chain rule: \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} 2(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) \cdot (-x_i) = 0\]


Factor out \(-2\), then divide both sides by \(-2\): \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 1: Linearity
Define weights \(c_i = \dfrac{x_i - \bar{x}}{S_{xx}}\). Then:
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{S_{xx}} = \frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})y_i}{S_{xx}} = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i\, y_i\]
The second equality holds because \(\sum(x_i - \bar{x})\bar{y} = \bar{y}\sum(x_i-\bar{x}) = 0\).
So \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) is a fixed linear combination of \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\) (the \(c_i\) depend only on \(x\), not \(y\)).
Since \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\), it is also linear in \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\). \(\blacksquare\)

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 2: Unbiasedness
Substitute the true model \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i\) into \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = \sum c_i y_i\):
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \sum c_i(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i) = \beta_0\underbrace{\sum c_i}_{=\,0} + \beta_1\underbrace{\sum c_i x_i}_{=\,1} + \sum c_i\varepsilon_i\]
The two key facts about \(c_i\):

\(\displaystyle\sum c_i = \frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})}{S_{xx}} = 0\)
\(\displaystyle\sum c_i x_i = \frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})x_i}{S_{xx}} = \frac{S_{xx}}{S_{xx}} = 1\)

So \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = \beta_1 + \sum c_i\varepsilon_i\), and since \(\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i)=0\): \(\;\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\). \(\blacksquare\)
For \(\widehat{\beta}_0\): \(\;\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \mathbb{E}(\bar{y}) - \beta_1\bar{x} = (\beta_0 + \beta_1\bar{x}) - \beta_1\bar{x} = \beta_0\). \(\blacksquare\)

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 3: Known Variances
From Property 2, \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = \beta_1 + \sum c_i\varepsilon_i\). Since \(\varepsilon_i\) are independent with \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\sigma^2\):
\[\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \sigma^2\sum c_i^2 = \sigma^2 \cdot \frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2}{S_{xx}^2} = \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} \qquad \blacksquare\]
For \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\), one can show \(\text{Cov}(\bar{y},\,\widehat{\beta}_1)=0\) (because \(\sum c_i = 0\)), so:
\[\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \text{Var}(\bar{y}) + \bar{x}^2\,\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} + \frac{\sigma^2\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}} = \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n}+\frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right) \qquad \blacksquare\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 4: Gauss-Markov (BLUE)

Goal: OLS has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators.
Let \(b_1^* = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i y_i\) be any competing linear unbiased estimator of \(\beta_1\).
Step 1 — unbiasedness constraints. We need \(\mathbb{E}(b_1^*) = \beta_1\) for all \(\beta_0, \beta_1\). Substitute \(\mathbb{E}(y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\): \[\mathbb{E}(b_1^*) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i) = \beta_0\sum_{i=1}^n c_i + \beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n c_i x_i\] For this to equal \(\beta_1\) for every possible \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\), we match coefficients: \[\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n c_i}_{\text{coeff. of }\beta_0} = 0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n c_i x_i}_{\text{coeff. of }\beta_1} = 1\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Why \(\mathbb{E}(\text{MSE}) = \sigma^2\)
Write each residual as \(e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i = \varepsilon_i - (\widehat{\beta}_0 - \beta_0) - (\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1)x_i\). A standard algebraic identity gives:
\[\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^2 - n(\bar{\varepsilon} )^2 - S_{xx}(\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1)^2\]
Taking expectations term by term, using \(\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i^2) = \sigma^2\), \(\mathbb{E}(\bar{\varepsilon}^2) = \sigma^2/n\), and \(\mathbb{E}[(\widehat{\beta}_1 - \beta_1)^2] = \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \sigma^2/S_{xx}\):
\[\mathbb{E}(\text{RSS}) = n\sigma^2 - n\cdot\frac{\sigma^2}{n} - S_{xx}\cdot\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} = n\sigma^2 - \sigma^2 - \sigma^2 = (n-2)\sigma^2\]
Dividing by \(n - 2\):
\[\mathbb{E}(\text{MSE}) = \frac{\mathbb{E}(\text{RSS})}{n-2} = \frac{(n-2)\sigma^2}{n-2} = \sigma^2 \qquad \blacksquare\]
The \(-2\) comes from estimating two parameters (\(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\)), each consuming one degree of freedom.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 1: \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) is Linear in \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\)
\(\widehat{\beta}_1\) is said to be a linear function of the responses if it is a linear combination \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n a_i y_i\), where the constants \(a_i\) do not depend on \(y_i\).
We can observe this starting with the OLS formula:
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i - \bar{x})^2}\]

Step 1 — split the numerator by expanding \((y_i - \bar{y})\):
\[= \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar{x})y_i \;-\; \sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar{x})\bar{y}}{S_{xx}}\]


Step 2 — drop the second term. Because deviations from the mean sum to zero (\(\sum(x_i-\bar{x})=0\)), and \(\bar{y}\) is a constant that factors out:
\[\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar{x})\bar{y} = \bar{y}\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar{x})}_{=\;0} = 0\]


Step 3 — identify the weights. Define \(a_i = \dfrac{x_i - \bar{x}}{S_{xx}}\). These depend only on the \(x_i\)’s, which are fixed constants, not on \(y\):
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar{x})\,y_i}{S_{xx}} = \sum_{i=1}^n \underbrace{\frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{S_{xx}}}_{a_i} y_i = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,y_i \quad \checkmark\]


For \(\widehat{\beta}_0\): write \(\bar{y} = \sum\frac{1}{n}y_i\) and substitute \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = \sum a_i y_i\). Collecting each \(y_i\) together:
\[\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x} = \sum_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{n}y_i - \bar{x}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i y_i = \sum_{i=1}^n\!\left(\frac{1}{n} - a_i\bar{x}\right)y_i \quad \checkmark\]
Thus both \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) are linear combinations of \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\). \(\blacksquare\)

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 2: \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) is Unbiased







Refresher: Expected Value


Key properties:

\(\mathbb{E}(c) = c\)
\(\mathbb{E}(aY) = a\,\mathbb{E}(Y)\)
\(\mathbb{E}(Y_1+Y_2)=\mathbb{E}(Y_1)+\mathbb{E}(Y_2)\)
\(\mathbb{E}\!\left(\sum_i a_i Y_i\right) = \sum_i a_i\,\mathbb{E}(Y_i)\)





Goal: show \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\), i.e. the estimator is correct on average.
From the model, \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i\) with \(\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i)=0\), so \(\mathbb{E}(y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\).

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 2: \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) is Unbiased
Goal: show \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \beta_0\).
Step 1 — find \(\mathbb{E}(\bar{y})\): expand using the model \(\mathbb{E}(y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\):
\[\mathbb{E}(\bar{y}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}(y_i) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i) = \frac{1}{n}(n\beta_0 + \beta_1 n\bar{x}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\bar{x}\]
Step 2 — apply linearity of expectation to \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\): since \(\bar{x}\) is a fixed constant,
\[\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \mathbb{E}(\bar{y}) - \bar{x}\,\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1)\]
Step 3 — substitute and cancel: plug in \(\mathbb{E}(\bar{y}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\bar{x}\) and \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\):
\[\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = (\beta_0 + \beta_1\bar{x}) - \bar{x}\,\beta_1 = \beta_0 \]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 3: Variance of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\)
Goal: derive the formula \(\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \sigma^2 / S_{xx}\).
Step 1 — apply the variance of a linear combination: since \(y_i\)’s are independent with \(\text{Var}(y_i)=\sigma^2\), and \(a_i\) are fixed constants:
\[\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \text{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i y_i\right) \overset{\text{indep.}}{=} \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\,\text{Var}(y_i) = \sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\]
Independence eliminates all cross-terms \(a_ia_j\text{Cov}(y_i,y_j)\) for \(i\neq j\).

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 3: Variance of \(\widehat{\beta}_0\)
Goal: derive \(\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \sigma^2\!\left(\tfrac{1}{n}+\tfrac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\).
Step 1 — expand the variance. Since \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\) and \(\bar{x}\) is a fixed constant:
\[\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \text{Var}(\bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}) = \text{Var}(\bar{y}) + \bar{x}^2\,\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) - 2\bar{x}\,\text{Cov}(\bar{y},\widehat{\beta}_1)\]
Step 2 — substitute known variances. Using \(\text{Var}(\bar{y}) = \sigma^2/n\) and \(\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \sigma^2/S_{xx}\):
\[= \frac{\sigma^2}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} - 2\bar{x}\,\text{Cov}(\bar{y},\widehat{\beta}_1)\]
Step 3 — handle the covariance. It can be shown that \(\text{Cov}(\bar{y}, \widehat{\beta}_1) = 0\) (see proof), so the last term drops out:
\[\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} = \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n}+\frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right) \qquad\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 1: Linearity of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\)

\(\widehat{\beta}_1\) is a linear combination \(\sum a_i y_i\) where weights \(a_i\) depend only on \(x\). Starting from: \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = \dfrac{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{S_{xx}}\)

Step 1 — split the numerator: \[= \frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})y_i \;-\; \sum(x_i-\bar{x})\bar{y}}{S_{xx}}\]


Step 2 — the second term is zero. Since \(\sum(x_i-\bar{x})=0\) (deviations from mean sum to zero) and \(\bar{y}\) is a constant: \[\sum(x_i-\bar{x})\bar{y} = \bar{y}\underbrace{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})}_{=\;0} = 0\]


Step 3 — define weights \(a_i = (x_i - \bar{x})/S_{xx}\), which depend only on \(x_i\): \[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})\,y_i}{S_{xx}} = \sum_{i=1}^n \underbrace{\frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{S_{xx}}}_{a_i} y_i = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,y_i \quad \checkmark\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 1: Linearity of \(\widehat{\beta}_0\)

From the previous slide, \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = \sum a_i y_i\). Now show \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\) is also linear.
Step 1 — write \(\bar{y}\) as a sum (the sample mean is itself a linear combination): \[\bar{y} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{n}y_i\]
Step 2 — substitute and collect \(y_i\) terms: \[\widehat{\beta}_0 = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{n}y_i - \bar{x}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i y_i = \sum_{i=1}^n\!\underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{n} - a_i\bar{x}\right)}_{\text{weight for }y_i}y_i\]
The weights \(\left(\tfrac{1}{n} - a_i\bar{x}\right)\) depend only on \(x_i\), not \(y_i\).
Both \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) are linear combinations of \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\).

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 2: \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) is Unbiased (cont.)

Since \(a_i\) are constants, linearity of expectation lets us pull them out: \[\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \mathbb{E}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i y_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,\mathbb{E}(y_i)\]
Substitute \(\mathbb{E}(y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\): \[= \sum_{i=1}^n a_i(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i) = \beta_0\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n a_i}_{=\,0} + \beta_1\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i}_{=\,1}\]
Why the sums equal 0 and 1: recall \(a_i = (x_i - \bar{x})/S_{xx}\)

\(\sum a_i = \sum(x_i-\bar{x})/S_{xx} = 0\) since deviations from the mean sum to zero
\(\sum a_i x_i = \sum(x_i-\bar{x})x_i/S_{xx} = S_{xx}/S_{xx} = 1\)

Therefore \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_0 \cdot 0 + \beta_1 \cdot 1 = \beta_1\).

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 3: Variance of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) (cont.)
Step 2 — evaluate \(\sum a_i^2\): substitute \(a_i = (x_i-\bar{x})/S_{xx}\) and use \(\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2 = S_{xx}\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(x_i-\bar{x})^2}{S_{xx}^2} = \frac{1}{S_{xx}^2}\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar{x})^2}_{=\,S_{xx}} = \frac{1}{S_{xx}}\]
Step 3 — combine:
\[\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \sigma^2 \cdot \frac{1}{S_{xx}} = \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} \qquad\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 3: Variance of \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) (cont.)
Step 3 — show \(\text{Cov}(\bar{y}, \widehat{\beta}_1) = 0\). Write both as linear combinations: \(\bar{y} = \sum \tfrac{1}{n}y_i\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = \sum a_i y_i\). By bilinearity of covariance:
\[\text{Cov}(\bar{y},\widehat{\beta}_1) = \sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n \frac{1}{n} \cdot a_j\, \text{Cov}(y_i, y_j)\]
Since \(y_i\)’s are independent, \(\text{Cov}(y_i, y_j) = 0\) for \(i \neq j\), so all off-diagonal terms vanish and only the \(i = j\) terms survive:
\[= \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{n} \cdot a_i \cdot \text{Var}(y_i) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n a_i}_{=\;0} = 0\]
using \(\sum a_i = 0\) (deviations from the mean always sum to zero).

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
\(\text{Cov}(\bar{y},\, \widehat{\beta}_1) = 0\)
Write both quantities as linear combinations of \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\):
\[\bar{y} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{n}\,y_i \qquad \widehat{\beta}_1 = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,y_i, \quad a_i = \frac{x_i-\bar{x}}{S_{xx}}\]
For two linear combinations of independent \(y_i\)’s, the covariance simplifies to:
\[\text{Cov}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n c_i\,y_i,\; \sum_{i=1}^n d_i\,y_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i\,d_i\,\text{Var}(y_i)\]
because all cross-terms \(\text{Cov}(y_i, y_j) = 0\) for \(i \neq j\) (independence). Applying this with \(c_i = 1/n\) and \(d_i = a_i\):
\[\text{Cov}(\bar{y},\,\widehat{\beta}_1) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{n}\cdot a_i \cdot \sigma^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} \cdot 0 = 0\]
The last step uses \(\sum a_i = 0\) (deviations from the mean always sum to zero). \(\blacksquare\)

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 3: Variance of \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) (cont.)
Conclusion — substitute \(\text{Cov}(\bar{y}, \widehat{\beta}_1) = 0\) back into Step 2:
\[\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} - 2\bar{x} \cdot 0 = \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n}+\frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right) \qquad \blacksquare\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 4: Gauss-Markov (BLUE) (cont.)

Step 2 — decompose the weights. Write \(c_i = a_i + d_i\), where \(a_i = (x_i-\bar{x})/S_{xx}\) are the OLS weights and \(d_i = c_i - a_i\) is the extra piece.
Both \(c_i\) and \(a_i\) satisfy the same two constraints:

From Step 1: \(\sum c_i = 0\) and \(\sum c_i x_i = 1\) (required for \(b_1^*\) to be unbiased)
From Property 1: \(\sum a_i = 0\) and \(\sum a_i x_i = 1\) (shown when we proved linearity of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\))

Subtracting gives \(\sum d_i = 0\) and \(\sum d_i x_i = 0\).

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 4: Gauss-Markov (BLUE) (cont.)

Step 2 (cont.) — show \(\sum a_i d_i = 0\). We need this so the cross term vanishes when we expand \(\sum(a_i + d_i)^2\) in Step 3 — without it we can’t isolate \(\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1)\). Using \(\sum d_i = 0\) and \(\sum d_i x_i = 0\): \[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i d_i = \frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})d_i}{S_{xx}} = \frac{\sum d_i x_i - \bar{x}\sum d_i}{S_{xx}} = \frac{0 - 0}{S_{xx}} = 0\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 4: Gauss-Markov (BLUE) (cont.)

Step 3 — compare variances. Two key rules:

\(\text{Var}(cY) = c^2\text{Var}(Y)\) — a constant scales variance by its square
\(\text{Var}(Y_1 + Y_2) = \text{Var}(Y_1) + \text{Var}(Y_2)\) when \(Y_1, Y_2\) are independent (cross terms \(2c_ic_j\text{Cov}(y_i,y_j) = 0\))

Applying both to \(b_1^* = \sum c_i y_i\) with independent \(y_i\)’s and \(\text{Var}(y_i) = \sigma^2\): \[\text{Var}(b_1^*) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2\,\text{Var}(y_i) = \sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 4: Gauss-Markov (BLUE) (cont.)

Substitute \(c_i = a_i + d_i\) and expand:
\[\sigma^2\sum(a_i + d_i)^2 = \sigma^2\!\left(\sum a_i^2 + 2\underbrace{\sum a_i d_i}_{=\;0} + \sum d_i^2\right) = \sigma^2\sum a_i^2 + \sigma^2\sum d_i^2\]
Recognizing \(\sigma^2 \sum a_i^2 = \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1)\):
\[\text{Var}(b_1^*) = \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) + \underbrace{\sigma^2 \sum d_i^2}_{\geq\;0} \;\geq\; \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) \qquad \]
The extra term \(\sigma^2\sum d_i^2 \geq 0\) always — with equality only when \(d_i = 0\) for all \(i\), i.e. when \(b_1^* = \widehat{\beta}_1\).

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text: Residuals

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
What are Residuals?
After fitting the model, the residual for observation \(i\) is:
\[e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i = y_i - \widehat{\beta}_0 - \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i\]
Residuals measure how far each observation falls from the fitted line:

\(e_i > 0\): observed value is above the fitted line
\(e_i < 0\): observed value is below the fitted line
\(e_i = 0\): observation falls exactly on the fitted line







Note


Residuals \(e_i\) are the observed counterparts to the unobservable errors \(\varepsilon_i\). We use them to check model assumptions and estimate \(\sigma^2\).

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Properties of OLS Residuals
The OLS normal equations force two exact constraints on the residuals:
\[\sum_{i=1}^n e_i = 0 \qquad \text{(1)}\]
\[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i e_i = 0 \qquad \text{(2)}\]
These two properties imply two more:

\(\bar{e} = 0\) — the mean of the residuals is always zero
\(\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{y}_i e_i = 0\) — residuals are uncorrelated with the fitted values







Note


These are exact algebraic facts — true for every OLS fit, regardless of whether the model is correct.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Proving the Properties
Property (1): \(\sum e_i = 0\). Recall normal equation 1: \[\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\beta}_0 - \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \sum_{i=1}^n e_i = 0\]
Property (2): \(\sum x_i e_i = 0\). Recall normal equation 2: \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i - \widehat{\beta}_0 - \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \sum_{i=1}^n x_i e_i = 0\]
Corollary: \(\sum \widehat{y}_i e_i = 0\). Since \(\widehat{y}_i = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i\): \[\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{y}_i e_i = \widehat{\beta}_0\underbrace{\sum e_i}_{=\,0} + \widehat{\beta}_1\underbrace{\sum x_i e_i}_{=\,0} = 0\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Residual Sum of Squares
The Residual Sum of Squares (RSS) measures the total unexplained variation:
\[\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{y}_i)^2\]

A smaller RSS means the line fits the data more closely
RSS = 0 only if every point lies exactly on the fitted line
RSS is used to estimate the unknown error variance \(\sigma^2\) (next lecture)







Note


RSS cannot be reduced further — OLS was specifically designed to minimize it.

From Monday, the simple linear regression model is:
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \quad \varepsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\]

\(\beta_1\) is a comparison between units
The fitted line \(\widehat{y} = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x\) summarizes the relationship

Today: How do we estimate \(\widehat{\beta}_0\), \(\widehat{\beta}_1\), and \(\sigma\) from data?

text:
Mini Refresher: Derivatives
Power rule: \(\frac{d}{dx} x^n = nx^{n-1}\)
Chain rule: \(\frac{d}{dx} f(g(x)) = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)\)
Partial derivatives: treat all other variables as constants and differentiate with respect to one variable at a time.
Example: \(\dfrac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0}(y - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x)^2 = 2(y - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x) \cdot (-1)\)

Mini Refresher: Summation Rules
Derivatives through sums: \[\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(\beta_0) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0} f_i(\beta_0)\]
Constants in sums:

\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n c = nc\) — a constant summed \(n\) times is just \(n \times c\)
\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n c \cdot x_i = c\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\) — a constant factor pulls out of the sum







Note


These are all we need to minimize RSS — apply the chain rule, pass the derivative through the sum, set to zero, and simplify.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
How do we pick \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\)?
We need a rule to pick the “best” \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\). To do so, we want to make prediction errors small across all observations simultaneously.
The residual for observation \(i\) is: \[e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i\]
where \(\widehat{y}_i\) is the predicted value \(\widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i\)
To find the best line, we minimize the Residual Sum of Squares: \[\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{y}_i)^2\]
We square the residuals so positive and negative errors don’t cancel, and so large errors are penalized more heavily.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
The Least Squares Criterion
From the previous slide, \(e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i\). Since the candidate line predicts \(\widehat{y}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\), substituting gives:
\[e_i = y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\]
So the Residual Sum of Squares is:
\[\text{RSS}(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2\]
Goal: choose \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) to minimize RSS.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
The Normal Equations
We have 2 unknowns (\(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\)) and need 2 equations to pin them down.
Setting \(\dfrac{\partial \text{RSS}}{\partial \beta_0} = 0\) and \(\dfrac{\partial \text{RSS}}{\partial \beta_1} = 0\) each gives one equation — together they form a system of two linear equations called the normal equations.
Recall: \(\text{RSS}(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2\)
Strategy: differentiate RSS with respect to each parameter, set each derivative to zero, then use the chain rule and summation rule to simplify.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
The Normal Equations: Derivation


Set \(\partial\text{RSS}/\partial\beta_0 = 0\): \[\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 = 0\]

Pass derivative through sum (summation rule): \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 = 0\]


Chain rule: \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} 2(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) \cdot (-1) = 0\]


Factor out \(-2\), then divide both sides by \(-2\): \[\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0\]


Set \(\partial\text{RSS}/\partial\beta_1 = 0\): \[\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 = 0\]

Pass derivative through sum (summation rule): \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_1}(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2 = 0\]


Chain rule: \[\sum_{i=1}^{n} 2(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) \cdot (-x_i) = 0\]


Factor out \(-2\), then divide both sides by \(-2\): \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Solving the Normal Equations: Step 1
Solve equation 1 for \(\widehat{\beta}_0\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; n\bar{y} - n\beta_0 - n\beta_1\bar{x} = 0\]
\[\boxed{\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}}\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Solving the Normal Equations: Step 2
Substitute into equation 2 and solve for \(\widehat{\beta}_1\):
Start with equation 2 and distribute the sum: \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - \beta_0\sum_{i=1}^n x_i - \beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 = 0\]
Substitute \(\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \beta_1\bar{x}\) and use \(\sum x_i = n\bar{x}\): \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - (\bar{y} - \beta_1\bar{x})\,n\bar{x} - \beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 = 0\]
Expand the multiplication: \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y} + n\bar{x}^2\beta_1 - \beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 = 0\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Solving the Normal Equations: Step 2 (cont.)
Collect \(\beta_1\) terms on the right: \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y} = \beta_1\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2\right)\]
Divide both sides by \(\left(\sum x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2\right)\):
\[\boxed{\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y}}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}}\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Equivalent Form of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\)
The numerator and denominator have a cleaner equivalent form. Expanding \(\sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})\):
\[\sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}) = \sum x_iy_i - \bar{y}\sum x_i - \bar{x}\sum y_i + n\bar{x}\bar{y}\]
Since \(\sum x_i = n\bar{x}\) and \(\sum y_i = n\bar{y}\):
\[= \sum x_iy_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y} - n\bar{x}\bar{y} + n\bar{x}\bar{y} = \sum x_iy_i - n\bar{x}\bar{y}\]
The same identity holds for the denominator: \(\displaystyle\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2 = \sum x_i^2 - n\bar{x}^2\)
So the two forms are equivalent. We will use the simpler form on the next slide.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
The OLS Estimators
Solving the normal equations yields:
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2} = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\]
\[\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\]
where:
\[S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}) \quad \text{(co-variation of } x \text{ and } y \text{ around their means)}\]
\[S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \quad \text{(total spread of } x \text{ around its mean)}\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Connection to Correlation
The OLS slope has a useful rewrite in terms of correlation:
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = r \cdot \frac{s_y}{s_x}\]
where \(r\) is the sample correlation between \(x\) and \(y\), and \(s_x\), \(s_y\) are sample standard deviations.

The sign of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) always equals the sign of \(r\)
When \(r = 0\) \(\rightarrow\) slope is 0 \(\rightarrow\) no linear relationship
When \(|r| = 1\) \(\rightarrow\) all points lie exactly on a line \(\rightarrow\) perfect fit

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Properties of the OLS Estimators

Notation: \(S_{xx} = \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i - \bar{x})^2\) — total spread of the predictor; \(\sigma^2\) — true (unknown) error variance; \(\mathbb{E}(\cdot)\) — expected value; \(\text{Var}(\cdot)\) — variance.


Linear: \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) are linear functions of \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\)
Unbiased: \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \beta_0\) and \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\) — on average, the estimates recover the true parameters
Known variances: \[\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\]
Gauss-Markov (BLUE): OLS has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators — no other such estimator can do better.

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 1: Linearity of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\)

\(\widehat{\beta}_1\) is a linear combination \(\sum a_i y_i\) where weights \(a_i\) depend only on \(x\). Starting from: \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = \dfrac{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{S_{xx}}\)

Step 1 — split the numerator: \[= \frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})y_i \;-\; \sum(x_i-\bar{x})\bar{y}}{S_{xx}}\]


Step 2 — the second term is zero. Since \(\sum(x_i-\bar{x})=0\) (deviations from mean sum to zero) and \(\bar{y}\) is a constant: \[\sum(x_i-\bar{x})\bar{y} = \bar{y}\underbrace{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})}_{=\;0} = 0\]


Step 3 — define weights \(a_i = (x_i - \bar{x})/S_{xx}\), which depend only on \(x_i\): \[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})\,y_i}{S_{xx}} = \sum_{i=1}^n \underbrace{\frac{x_i - \bar{x}}{S_{xx}}}_{a_i} y_i = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,y_i \quad \checkmark\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 1: Linearity of \(\widehat{\beta}_0\)

From the previous slide, \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = \sum a_i y_i\). Now show \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\) is also linear.
Step 1 — write \(\bar{y}\) as a sum (the sample mean is itself a linear combination): \[\bar{y} = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{n}y_i\]
Step 2 — substitute and collect \(y_i\) terms: \[\widehat{\beta}_0 = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{n}y_i - \bar{x}\sum_{i=1}^n a_i y_i = \sum_{i=1}^n\!\underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{n} - a_i\bar{x}\right)}_{\text{weight for }y_i}y_i\]
The weights \(\left(\tfrac{1}{n} - a_i\bar{x}\right)\) depend only on \(x_i\), not \(y_i\).
Both \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) are linear combinations of \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\).

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 2: \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) is Unbiased







Refresher: Expected Value


Key properties:

\(\mathbb{E}(c) = c\)
\(\mathbb{E}(aY) = a\,\mathbb{E}(Y)\)
\(\mathbb{E}(Y_1+Y_2)=\mathbb{E}(Y_1)+\mathbb{E}(Y_2)\)
\(\mathbb{E}\!\left(\sum_i a_i Y_i\right) = \sum_i a_i\,\mathbb{E}(Y_i)\)





Goal: show \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\), i.e. the estimator is correct on average.
From the model, \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i\) with \(\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i)=0\), so \(\mathbb{E}(y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\).

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 2: \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) is Unbiased (cont.)

Since \(a_i\) are constants, linearity of expectation lets us pull them out: \[\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \mathbb{E}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i y_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i\,\mathbb{E}(y_i)\]
Substitute \(\mathbb{E}(y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\): \[= \sum_{i=1}^n a_i(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i) = \beta_0\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n a_i}_{=\,0} + \beta_1\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i}_{=\,1}\]
Why the sums equal 0 and 1: recall \(a_i = (x_i - \bar{x})/S_{xx}\)

\(\sum a_i = \sum(x_i-\bar{x})/S_{xx} = 0\) since deviations from the mean sum to zero
\(\sum a_i x_i = \sum(x_i-\bar{x})x_i/S_{xx} = S_{xx}/S_{xx} = 1\)

Therefore \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_0 \cdot 0 + \beta_1 \cdot 1 = \beta_1\).

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 2: \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) is Unbiased
Goal: show \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \beta_0\).
Step 1 — find \(\mathbb{E}(\bar{y})\): expand using the model \(\mathbb{E}(y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\):
\[\mathbb{E}(\bar{y}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}(y_i) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i) = \frac{1}{n}(n\beta_0 + \beta_1 n\bar{x}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\bar{x}\]
Step 2 — apply linearity of expectation to \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\): since \(\bar{x}\) is a fixed constant,
\[\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \mathbb{E}(\bar{y}) - \bar{x}\,\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1)\]
Step 3 — substitute and cancel: plug in \(\mathbb{E}(\bar{y}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\bar{x}\) and \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \beta_1\):
\[\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = (\beta_0 + \beta_1\bar{x}) - \bar{x}\,\beta_1 = \beta_0 \]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 3: Variance of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\)
Goal: derive the formula \(\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \sigma^2 / S_{xx}\).
Step 1 — apply the variance of a linear combination: since \(y_i\)’s are independent with \(\text{Var}(y_i)=\sigma^2\), and \(a_i\) are fixed constants:
\[\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \text{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i y_i\right) \overset{\text{indep.}}{=} \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\,\text{Var}(y_i) = \sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\]
Independence eliminates all cross-terms \(a_ia_j\text{Cov}(y_i,y_j)\) for \(i\neq j\).

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 3: Variance of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) (cont.)
Step 2 — evaluate \(\sum a_i^2\): substitute \(a_i = (x_i-\bar{x})/S_{xx}\) and use \(\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2 = S_{xx}\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(x_i-\bar{x})^2}{S_{xx}^2} = \frac{1}{S_{xx}^2}\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar{x})^2}_{=\,S_{xx}} = \frac{1}{S_{xx}}\]
Step 3 — combine:
\[\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \sigma^2 \cdot \frac{1}{S_{xx}} = \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} \qquad\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 3: Variance of \(\widehat{\beta}_0\)
Goal: derive \(\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \sigma^2\!\left(\tfrac{1}{n}+\tfrac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\).
Step 1 — expand the variance. Since \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\) and \(\bar{x}\) is a fixed constant:
\[\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \text{Var}(\bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}) = \text{Var}(\bar{y}) + \bar{x}^2\,\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) - 2\bar{x}\,\text{Cov}(\bar{y},\widehat{\beta}_1)\]
Step 2 — substitute known variances. Using \(\text{Var}(\bar{y}) = \sigma^2/n\) and \(\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \sigma^2/S_{xx}\):
\[= \frac{\sigma^2}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} - 2\bar{x}\,\text{Cov}(\bar{y},\widehat{\beta}_1)\]
Step 3 — handle the covariance. It can be shown that \(\text{Cov}(\bar{y}, \widehat{\beta}_1) = 0\) (see proof), so the last term drops out:
\[\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} = \sigma^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n}+\frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right) \qquad\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 4: Gauss-Markov (BLUE)

Goal: OLS has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators.
Let \(b_1^* = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i y_i\) be any competing linear unbiased estimator of \(\beta_1\).
Step 1 — unbiasedness constraints. We need \(\mathbb{E}(b_1^*) = \beta_1\) for all \(\beta_0, \beta_1\). Substitute \(\mathbb{E}(y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\): \[\mathbb{E}(b_1^*) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i) = \beta_0\sum_{i=1}^n c_i + \beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n c_i x_i\] For this to equal \(\beta_1\) for every possible \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\), we match coefficients: \[\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n c_i}_{\text{coeff. of }\beta_0} = 0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n c_i x_i}_{\text{coeff. of }\beta_1} = 1\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 4: Gauss-Markov (BLUE) (cont.)

Step 2 — decompose the weights. Write \(c_i = a_i + d_i\), where \(a_i = (x_i-\bar{x})/S_{xx}\) are the OLS weights and \(d_i = c_i - a_i\) is the extra piece.
Both \(c_i\) and \(a_i\) satisfy the same two constraints:

From Step 1: \(\sum c_i = 0\) and \(\sum c_i x_i = 1\) (required for \(b_1^*\) to be unbiased)
From Property 1: \(\sum a_i = 0\) and \(\sum a_i x_i = 1\) (shown when we proved linearity of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\))

Subtracting gives \(\sum d_i = 0\) and \(\sum d_i x_i = 0\).

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 4: Gauss-Markov (BLUE) (cont.)

Step 2 (cont.) — show \(\sum a_i d_i = 0\). We need this so the cross term vanishes when we expand \(\sum(a_i + d_i)^2\) in Step 3 — without it we can’t isolate \(\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1)\). Using \(\sum d_i = 0\) and \(\sum d_i x_i = 0\): \[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i d_i = \frac{\sum(x_i-\bar{x})d_i}{S_{xx}} = \frac{\sum d_i x_i - \bar{x}\sum d_i}{S_{xx}} = \frac{0 - 0}{S_{xx}} = 0\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 4: Gauss-Markov (BLUE) (cont.)

Step 3 — compare variances. Two key rules:

\(\text{Var}(cY) = c^2\text{Var}(Y)\) — a constant scales variance by its square
\(\text{Var}(Y_1 + Y_2) = \text{Var}(Y_1) + \text{Var}(Y_2)\) when \(Y_1, Y_2\) are independent (cross terms \(2c_ic_j\text{Cov}(y_i,y_j) = 0\))

Applying both to \(b_1^* = \sum c_i y_i\) with independent \(y_i\)’s and \(\text{Var}(y_i) = \sigma^2\): \[\text{Var}(b_1^*) = \sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2\,\text{Var}(y_i) = \sigma^2\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2\]

title: Lecture 2: Fitting the Simple Linear Model
text:
Property 4: Gauss-Markov (BLUE) (cont.)

Substitute \(c_i = a_i + d_i\) and expand:
\[\sigma^2\sum(a_i + d_i)^2 = \sigma^2\!\left(\sum a_i^2 + 2\underbrace{\sum a_i d_i}_{=\;0} + \sum d_i^2\right) = \sigma^2\sum a_i^2 + \sigma^2\sum d_i^2\]
Recognizing \(\sigma^2 \sum a_i^2 = \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1)\):
\[\text{Var}(b_1^*) = \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) + \underbrace{\sigma^2 \sum d_i^2}_{\geq\;0} \;\geq\; \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) \qquad \]
The extra term \(\sigma^2\sum d_i^2 \geq 0\) always — with equality only when \(d_i = 0\) for all \(i\), i.e. when \(b_1^* = \widehat{\beta}_1\).

title: Lecture 3: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Summary

Residuals \(e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i\) are observed proxies for the unobservable errors \(\varepsilon_i\)
Five properties of OLS residuals follow from the normal equations: \(\sum e_i = 0\), \(\sum \widehat{y}_i = \sum y_i\), \(\sum x_i e_i = 0\), \(\sum \widehat{y}_i e_i = 0\), and the line passes through \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\)
RSS \(= \sum e_i^2\) measures total unexplained variation — OLS minimizes it by construction
\(\widehat{\sigma}^2 = \text{RSS}/(n-2)\) is an unbiased estimate of \(\sigma^2\); dividing by \(n-2\) corrects for two constraints placed on the residuals
\(\widehat{\sigma}\) is the residual standard deviation — the typical prediction error on the scale of \(y\)
Standard errors replace \(\sigma\) with \(\widehat{\sigma}\) in the variance formulas — the foundation for inference

text:
Review: OLS Estimators
From last time, the OLS estimators are:
\[\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\]
They are unbiased, linear, and BLUE (Gauss-Markov).
Today: What do the residuals tell us, and how do we estimate the unknown \(\sigma^2\)?

title: Lecture 3: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text: Residuals

title: Lecture 3: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
What are Residuals?
After fitting the model, the residual for observation \(i\) is:
\[e_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i = y_i - \widehat{\beta}_0 - \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i\]
Residuals measure how far each observation falls from the fitted line:

\(e_i > 0\): observed value is above the fitted line
\(e_i < 0\): observed value is below the fitted line
\(e_i = 0\): observation falls exactly on the fitted line







Note


Residuals \(e_i\) are the observable counterparts to the unobservable errors \(\varepsilon_i\). We use them to check model assumptions and estimate \(\sigma^2\).

title: Lecture 3: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Properties of OLS Residuals

\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n e_i = 0\) — residuals sum to zero
\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{y}_i = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i\) — sum of fitted values equals sum of observed values
\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_i e_i = 0\) — residuals are uncorrelated with the predictor
\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{y}_i e_i = 0\) — residuals are uncorrelated with the fitted values
The fitted line always passes through \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\)

title: Lecture 3: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Proving the Properties

Property (1): \(\sum e_i = 0\). Directly from normal equation 1: \[\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{\beta}_0 - \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \sum_{i=1}^n e_i = 0\]
Property (2): \(\sum \widehat{y}_i = \sum y_i\). Since \(\sum e_i = \sum(y_i - \widehat{y}_i) = 0\), rearranging gives \(\sum \widehat{y}_i = \sum y_i\).
Property (3): \(\sum x_i e_i = 0\). Directly from normal equation 2: \[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i - \widehat{\beta}_0 - \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; \sum_{i=1}^n x_i e_i = 0\]
Property (4): \(\sum \widehat{y}_i e_i = 0\). Since \(\widehat{y}_i = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i\): \[\sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{y}_i e_i = \widehat{\beta}_0\underbrace{\sum e_i}_{=\,0} + \widehat{\beta}_1\underbrace{\sum x_i e_i}_{=\,0} = 0\]
Property (5): line passes through \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\). From \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\): \[\widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x} = \bar{y} \checkmark\]

title: Lecture 3: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text: Estimating \(\sigma^2\)

title: Lecture 3: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Residual Sum of Squares
The Residual Sum of Squares (RSS) measures the total unexplained variation:
\[\text{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{y}_i)^2\]

A smaller RSS means the line fits the data more closely
RSS = 0 only if every point lies exactly on the fitted line

title: Lecture 3: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Estimating \(\sigma^2\)
The error variance \(\sigma^2 = \text{Var}(\varepsilon_i)\) is unknown. We estimate it using the residuals.
A natural starting point is the average squared residual, but we must divide by \(n - 2\), not \(n\):
\[\widehat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\text{RSS}}{n - 2} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2}{n-2}\]
Why \(n - 2\)? Estimating \(\widehat{\beta}_0\) and \(\widehat{\beta}_1\) uses 2 degrees of freedom since two parameters are being used.
It can be shown that \(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\sigma}^2) = \sigma^2\), so \(\widehat{\sigma}^2\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\).

title: Lecture 3: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
The Residual Standard Deviation
Taking the square root gives the residual standard deviation:
\[\widehat{\sigma} = \sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}^2} = \sqrt{\frac{\text{RSS}}{n-2}}\]
Interpretation: \(\widehat{\sigma}\) is the typical size of a prediction error, on the scale of \(y\).






Tip


Compare \(\widehat{\sigma}\) to the spread of \(y\) to gauge model usefulness. A small \(\widehat{\sigma}\) relative to the range of \(y\) indicates a good fit.

title: Lecture 3: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Standard Errors of the Estimators
Since \(\sigma^2\) is unknown, we replace it with \(\widehat{\sigma}^2\) in the variance formulas:
\[\widehat{\text{Var}}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\widehat{\sigma}^2}{S_{xx}}, \qquad \widehat{\text{Var}}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \widehat{\sigma}^2\!\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}\right)\]
The standard errors are the square roots:
\[\text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\widehat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}, \qquad \text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_0) = \widehat{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{S_{xx}}}\]
Standard errors quantify the uncertainty in each estimate — they are the basis for confidence intervals and hypothesis tests (coming soon).

\(\widehat{\sigma}^2 = \text{RSS} / (n - 2)\)
\(\widehat{\sigma} = \sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}^2}\)
\(\text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \widehat{\sigma} / \sqrt{S_{xx}}\)

title: Lecture 3: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Practice: Solution
Step 1 — estimate \(\sigma^2\): \[\widehat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\text{RSS}}{n-2} = \frac{6}{5-2} = \frac{6}{3} = 2\]
Step 2 — residual standard deviation: \[\widehat{\sigma} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41\]
Step 3 — standard error of \(\widehat{\beta}_1\): \[\text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\widehat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{10}} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{10}} = \sqrt{0.2} \approx 0.45\]
Interpretation: the slope estimate \(\widehat{\beta}_1 = 2\) has a typical uncertainty of about \(\pm 0.45\) wellness points per hour of exercise.

title: Lecture 3: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Proof: \(\mathbb{E}(\text{MSE}) = \sigma^2\)

Step 1 — expand E(SSE). Substitute \(\widehat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1\bar{x}\): \[\mathbb{E}(\text{SSE}) = \mathbb{E}\!\left\{\sum(y_i - \widehat{y}_i)^2\right\} = \mathbb{E}\!\left\{\sum\!\left[(y_i - \bar{y}) - \widehat{\beta}_1(x_i - \bar{x})\right]^2\right\}\]
Step 2 — expand the square and use \(\sum(y_i-\bar{y})(x_i-\bar{x}) = \widehat{\beta}_1 S_{xx}\): \[= \mathbb{E}\!\left\{\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2 + \widehat{\beta}_1^2 S_{xx} - 2\widehat{\beta}_1^2 S_{xx}\right\} = \mathbb{E}\!\left\{\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2 - \widehat{\beta}_1^2 S_{xx}\right\}\]

title: Lecture 3: Residuals and Estimating Error Variance
text:
Proof: \(\mathbb{E}(\text{MSE}) = \sigma^2\) (cont.)

Step 3 — evaluate each expectation piece by piece.
Substitute \(y_i - \bar{y} = \beta_1(x_i-\bar{x}) + (\varepsilon_i - \bar{\varepsilon})\) and expand:

\(\mathbb{E}\!\left\{\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2\right\} = \beta_1^2 S_{xx} + \mathbb{E}\!\left\{\sum(\varepsilon_i-\bar{\varepsilon})^2\right\} + 0 = \beta_1^2 S_{xx} + (n-1)\sigma^2\)
since \(\mathbb{E}\!\left\{\sum(\varepsilon_i - \bar{\varepsilon})^2\right\} = (n-1)\sigma^2\) and the cross term has \(\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i - \bar{\varepsilon}) = 0\)
\(\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1^2) = \text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1) + \left[\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1)\right]^2 = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} + \beta_1^2\), so \(\;\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1^2 S_{xx}) = \sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{xx}\)

Step 4 — combine: \[\mathbb{E}(\text{SSE}) = \beta_1^2 S_{xx} + (n-1)\sigma^2 - \sigma^2 - \beta_1^2 S_{xx} = (n-2)\sigma^2\]
Therefore: \[\mathbb{E}(\text{MSE}) = \mathbb{E}\!\left(\frac{\text{SSE}}{n-2}\right) = \frac{(n-2)\sigma^2}{n-2} = \sigma^2 \qquad \blacksquare\]
